title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training

details.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
details.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand

details.title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
details.abstract: Evaluating models on full benchmarks is often expensive. Benchmark compression reduces this cost by using small subsets to approximate full-benchmark results. This paper theoretically explains why random sampling works surprisingly well for benchmark compression but can be unstable, and introduces BestRand, a simple, stable, and low-cost solution. Across 70+ benchmarks, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4%, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost of competing methods.

title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents

details.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
details.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EVOMEMSTATE consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git .

title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents

details.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
details.abstract: VisSearch-Bench evaluates how multimodal agents organize and use visual evidence during long-horizon web search. It contains 204 human-written tasks across five search categories, spanning 7 domains and 25 subdomains. The tasks require agents to connect information across images, objects, and search steps to compare candidates, follow visual clues, and produce complete answers. Each task includes a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Evaluation measures both full task success and the correctness and completeness of individual results. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, highlighting the challenge of managing visual context even with search tools.

title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex

details.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
details.abstract: We present Drex, a family of four open decision models that return a calibrated probability distribution over user-defined options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Each request pairs a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) with questions asking for a choice, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. The family spans 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B-A3B (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with our in-house RL recipe, reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), which blends verified outcomes with a reasoning judge under a KL constraint; ablations show RLAF raises accuracy while consistency losses cut option-order flips from 6.3% to 4.2%. Drex Max sets a new state of the art among decision models on Decision Index 0.4.1 (67.52 vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0) and holds its score on maintainer-run private tests (66.60). On the independently run Artificial Analysis Decision Index, Max has the second-highest score among decision models, and Drex is among the most widely used decision models on OpenRouter. All weights and inference code are open: github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer

details.title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
details.abstract: How much can a small model benefit from a larger model that only processes the prompt—and what actually drives the improvement? We explore these questions in this new paper. In prefill-to-autoregressive cross-model transfer (PACT), a larger sender processes the prompt and passes internal representations to a smaller receiver, which then generates the response independently. We introduce PLatour, a simple and scalable framework that connects frozen models through lightweight linear bridges trained directly with reinforcement learning. It also supports hybrid-attention architectures. On generation tasks, PLatour substantially outperforms the evaluated open-source PACT baselines. Using a 35B sender, it also exceeds Mostik AI’s reported results on shared math and coding benchmarks, compared with Mostik's 753B sender—although the training setups may differ. But stronger benchmark results do not, by themselves, establish useful information transfer. On some tasks, replacing sender representations with question-independent signals or training the receiver alone reproduces much of the improvement. Trainable bridges can provide substantial adaptation capacity even when both model backbones are frozen. The evidence is task-dependent: controls nearly match PLatour on GSM8K, while PLatour retains gains beyond all tested controls on Chemistry with chain-of-thought generation. To examine this systematically, we introduce PACT-Check. It combines interventions on sender information with separately trained adaptation baselines. PACT-Score measures the accuracy margin over the strongest applicable control. Our takeaway: PACT shows promising performance, but understanding its benefits requires distinguishing useful sender information from gains achievable through adaptation. We hope PLatour and PACT-Check help the community investigate when prefill-only communication helps—and how to make those benefits more reliable.

title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models

details.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
details.abstract: Hi everyone! We’re the authors of Open-HumanWAM , an open recipe for scaling human and robot experience for embodied foundation models. We study how human experience can improve robot learning, using Open-HumanWAM-50K , a 50,000-hour egocentric corpus with hand-motion and language annotations. 📈 HumanWAM-Vanilla — scaling human experience: our exploration studies show that scaling egocentric pretraining improves generalization to unseen scenes and randomized environments. Greater data diversity strengthens the scaling trend, while human pretraining improves robot demonstration efficiency. The final model achieves 92.08% Clean / 68.88% Random , averaging 80.48% on RoboTwin 2.0 . 🤖 HumanWAM-Goal — zero-shot transfer: combining human and robot experience improves zero-shot generalization in simulation and the real world. Visual goals enable robots to follow human demonstrations and adapt their behavior through in-context conditioning, without target-task parameter updates. 🏆 RoboTwin 2.0 Rank #1: after post-training, HumanWAM-Goal achieves 92.70% Clean / 84.60% Random , averaging 88.65% . We’re releasing the corpus, checkpoints, and code, with uploads and documentation updates ongoing. We’d love to hear your thoughts and questions! 🌐 Project & demos · 💻 Code · 🤗 Corpus · 🤗 Models

title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation

details.title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation
details.abstract: 🤖 HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation How can robots track task progress when the current observation alone is insufficient? We introduce HeLM, a hierarchical VLM–VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language memory. Two key aspects of our work: 🧠 Event-triggered memory updates: HeLM separates visual event detection from memory updates. The HLP updates memory and generates the next action command only when a task-relevant event is detected or the instruction changes. 🔄 Inter-episode memory: We introduce tasks where robots must remember information acquired under previous instructions, such as a human-demonstrated button sequence. We evaluate HeLM on 10 real-world non-Markovian tasks (56 variants) . Our two-stage inference improves average intra-episode subtask success from 67.7% to 85.7% compared with a one-stage variant. We also provide detailed failure analyses and evaluations of memory scalability. We welcome feedback and discussions on memory for robot learning!

title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models

details.title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models
details.abstract: Can we scale up imagination-free WAMs (e.g., Fast-WAM)? Excited to share DreamFree — an imagination-free WAM that improves with stronger video models and more video data, running at 11 Hz with a 14B video backbone. Video models learn how the world changes, providing useful knowledge for robot control. But generating future videos is costly, and prediction errors can affect actions. Imagination-free WAMs, e.g., Fast-WAM, enable robot control without generating future videos. But for Fast-WAM, stronger video priors don't automatically mean better control. In our experiments, scaling from 5B to 14B did not improve success. How can we make imagination-free WAMs benefit from stronger video models? Our key idea: turn the pretrained video model into a predictive visual encoder A frozen video teacher sees the future. The encoder learns to predict the teacher’s representation from the current view. This teaches the encoder to anticipate scene changes without generating future videos. Training the encoder needs only videos, without using action labels. Next, we train the action DiT using robot demonstrations with action labels. From the encoder’s visual representation, a readout learns to extract action-relevant information. An action decoder uses this information to predict robot actions. What we find: Real-world performance: Trained on DROID alone, DreamFree achieves 64% success across 10 real-world tasks, outperforming DreamZero at 56% and π0.5 at 16%. We evaluate the policies without task-specific fine-tuning. Fast inference: A 14B video backbone runs at 11 Hz on a single H200, with 17.8× faster inference than DreamZero. Memory efficiency: With a 14B video backbone, DreamFree fits on a single A6000 GPU with 48 GB of memory, without future-video generation or classifier-free guidance at inference. Better scaling: Scaling the video backbone from 5B to 14B significantly improves performance, enabling real-world manipulation on DROID and bimanual YAM. More video data further improves control without additional action labels. Video-only task transfer: DreamFree learns new task sequences from videos, including demonstrations from a different robot embodiment, without action labels for the new tasks.

title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization

details.title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization
details.abstract: TL;DR : We train a TopK SAE with 2^20 latents and k = 100 on the MoE block output of Qwen3-30B-A3B at layers 4, 30 and 46. Because the SAE encoder is affine and the MoE output is a weighted sum of expert outputs, the activation of each latent decomposes exactly over the activated experts. Aggregating this decomposition over 1.5B tokens gives every expert a dominant set of latents that it principally drives. This lets us read what each expert does without any predefined domain taxonomy. Key findings: Contribution is far more concentrated than gating. Most latents have only one or two dominators. Dominant sets are largely private to each expert. Experts specialize below coarse domains. A Java expert sits next to a separate expert for front end web code, and a geometry expert sits next to one for arithmetic and polynomials. Grouping the 128 experts of layer 30 gives 11 domains of very unequal size. Some domains are not subject areas at all, such as text form, language, and entities and identifiers. Code, the three SAEs, and an interactive explorer of all 128 experts of layer 30 are released. Happy to answer questions!

title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence

details.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
details.abstract: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence For a decade, AI progress has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Agents now write code and run multistep tasks for us, yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, and face hard choices without their own history. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot. This perspective paper argues that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance: the person augmented by AI. What the paper covers: 🧠 AHI alongside AGI: AGI asks how intelligent a machine can be; AI-Augmented Human Intelligence (AHI) asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. 🎧 The cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, and takes part in their thinking at the right moment. 📏 The cognitive gap: the conceptual core, the distance between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory. 🔄 The symbiosis loop: sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. 🪜 A ladder of assistance: getting things done, thinking and feeling with the person, and living among others with the person, up to the meeting of two symbionts. ⚖️ Risk and governance: from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, with 23 open problems and the conditions that would prove the paper wrong. 🌐 Project page: https://cognitive-symbiont.github.io Feedback and discussion are very welcome!

title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models

details.title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models
details.abstract: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Full-Duplex Speech Language Models Most existing full-duplex speech models alternate between listening and speaking in fixed time chunks, which leaves the load across chunks highly uneven: compute sits idle during "listening", while "speaking" and tool calls miss their deadlines and fall behind because they generate many tokens serially. We observe that with silence as the hypothesized input, the output of 95.3% of chunks is identical to the output produced from the real audio, and 88% of divergences appear at the very first token. Building on this, Speculative Listening uses the idle compute of listening to draft the next chunk before the real audio arrives, using silence and the runner-up first-token candidate. All drafts are then verified together once the audio arrives, which requires no additional training and guarantees lossless output. Speed: On TickTock-Bench, the eight-task evaluation suite we built, speaking chunks are accelerated by 2.6–2.8×, and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4×. Latency: Decoding latency before a response begins drops by 73% on average, to 74–241 ms, close to the 200 ms turn-taking gap in human conversation. The maximum lag behind real time is reduced by 94.4%.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

details.title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
details.abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset

details.title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset
details.abstract: Face datasets are heavily skewed across age, race and gender, and large real-world collections include people who never agreed to be used for training. We propose SynthFaces, a synthetic alternative that is balanced by design. A label-conditional flow matching model, ID-Flow, samples new identities for any chosen demographic group. An identity-conditioned generator turns them into face images, which are then placed into varied, captioned scenes. The result is a large dataset of non-existent people, with about 10 images per identity. It can be used to train and fine-tune fairer identity-preserving models without real personal data. Accepted to BMVC 2026.

title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents

details.title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
details.abstract: We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM) , an architecture that turns historical experience into predictions for agent decisions through a shared pretrained learner. The key idea is to separate semantic representation from empirical inference. An LLM represents current and historical records, while a conditional predictor uses the represented evidence to predict task-defined targets. This brings together two complementary capabilities: semantic knowledge from language pretraining and empirical inference from structured-data pretraining. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share the same evidence-and-query interface, with predictions converted into choices by a decision rule. We use a single frozen LimiX-2 predictor across all five evaluated task categories, without updating either model’s neural parameters at deployment. Key results: Across 50 benchmarks: With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, mean accuracy rises from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% with DPDM at the methods’ respective evaluated history budgets. With identical histories and queries, DPDM reaches 82.33% . Tool-use assessment: On ToolPRMBench’s BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, accuracy improves over few-shot prompting by 34.26 and 28.87 percentage points , respectively, at the methods’ respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy also improves as history grows. Imbalanced histories: With identical imbalanced histories, DPDM improves mean balanced accuracy over few-shot prompting by 14.51 percentage points across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability: advances in a shared conditional predictor can improve decisions across agent tasks. We welcome feedback and discussion!

title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks

details.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
details.abstract: I'll tell you what, only 27% of model pairs kept the same best attack template after a new pretraining seed, against 67% after a new post-training seed. For a bank that buys a vendor model and gets silent base-model refreshes, that reads like a red-team result is tied to one pretraining run, not to the model name on the contract. Is that how you would read it? And could the fingerprint work as a cheap, FAST check? If a random 50 prompts identify the pretraining run 98% of the time among your 75 runs, a "same model" update that no longer matches would be the signal that a full re-test is due.
